investigations.headline: How The Rivalries Were Counted
investigations.subhead: Every rivalry ranking this desk has published rests on one number. Here is that number for all sixteen managers, the eight figures behind it, and everything it cannot do.
investigations.byline: The SCFL NewsRoom · The Record Room
paragraphs: A volley is two managers speaking back to back: one posts, a different one answers within 7 minutes, and that is one volley on their shared account. It is a deliberately dumb measure. It cannot read a room, it does not know who was addressing whom in a crowd, and it counts a joke exactly as heavily as a grievance.
What it is good at is the part that matters: it is symmetrical, it needs no interpretation, and nobody can lobby it. Two managers cannot volley without both of them showing up.

The figure the rankings use is not the raw count. It is the mutual share — the geometric mean of the two sides’ attention. If a pairing is 20 per cent of your talk and 4 per cent of his, the mutual figure is 9, not 12. A geometric mean punishes lopsidedness on purpose, because one man shouting at another man is not a rivalry.

One number on this page does not mean what the other fifteen mean. The Jet-I left the Mos Eisley chat on 5 June 2022 and has not posted in it since. He did not leave the league. He is still in it, still drafting, and still in the league chat, where his most recent message is dated 17 August 2026. The reasons he walked out of the room were not fantasy football, and they are not this desk’s business.

What is this desk’s business is that every figure here counts the room he stopped standing in. His 3,408 volleys are not a measure of how much he talks; they are a measure of when he stopped. Read every JET row as a floor, and read his splits with more suspicion still — a small denominator makes any pairing look like an obsession, which is exactly why he takes two of the top four rows in Figure Three.

A volley is proximity, not address. In a fast group chat two managers can volley for an hour without once speaking to each other. It cannot see a reply posted eleven minutes late, and it weighs a joke exactly as heavily as a grievance.

Replies are not in the file at all. WhatsApp’s text export carries the sender, the timestamp and the text and nothing else — a swipe-to-reply arrives as an ordinary message with no link back to the one it answered. That thread structure would be the best evidence here and it does not survive the export, which is why a seven-minute window is doing the work instead.

Presence is not temperament. The measure assumes the sixteen are all standing in the same room, and one of them has not been for years. Where that is true the page says so with a dagger, but there is no correction that fixes it: you cannot infer the volleys a man would have thrown had he stayed.

Sourcing: the league chats, May 2021 to August 2026. The volley definition is the same code path as scripts/build_rivalries.py, so this documents the ranking rather than describing a different measure. Only aggregate counts are published: the build checks the rendered page against all 292,417 messages and refuses to write if any run of thirty characters survives into it. The corpus is not in this repository and never will be.

investigations.headline: Nine to Six, and the Wire Stays Shut
investigations.subhead: The freeze began with two words about Carson Beck and ended with the league voting to do exactly what the calendar already said. In between, a vote called off the calendar turned every settled rule into an open question.
investigations.byline: The SCFL NewsRoom · The Politics Desk
paragraphs: The waiver wire opens on August 25 and clears on the 26th, which is where it was always going to open before anybody moved anything. It took a month-long standoff, a disputed flash poll, a formal vote and one correction that cost the man who made it his own argument to arrive back at the date the league already had.

HOW IT STARTED — It began with two words. Mid-column on his draft grades, the Powers of Pain noticed a transaction and asked the Horse Collars whether he was really cutting Carson Beck already. The reply was “Umm. Waiver wire.” A cut player has to land somewhere, and after a draft moved up to July 24 — weeks ahead of the league's traditional window — nobody had decided where, or when anyone was allowed to pick him up. The league office froze the wire that afternoon.

THE ARGUMENT — The open-the-wire side held that the wire is the counterbalance to an early draft, and that holding rosters static for a month would produce, in effect, a second draft in late August. The traditionalists held that the fix for one broken date is not to break a second one. Underneath the mechanics sat a procedural objection the Smoke Dragons made repeatedly and, in the end, decisively: that a change this size does not belong in a chat poll at all. “We vote at the draft. That's how we handle these things.”

THE BALLOT KEPT MOVING — This league votes on draft day. That is the whole of the procedure and it is the reason the Smoke Dragons kept objecting to the form rather than the substance: “Changing the draft and waivers is a way bigger deal than just a flash vote on the chat.” This vote was called in a chat, a fortnight out, and for most of that fortnight nobody could say with confidence what was going to be on it.

Still The Creamiest asked the question everybody else was too dug in to ask. On July 25, one day into the argument: “So is this vote for daily waivers or just to open up waivers early?” He had a clear position and nowhere to put it — “I don't want daily waivers. I don't mind opening up the waivers early and making it weekly waivers from now” — and he spent that afternoon asking somebody to write the thing down. “Make that a voting poll.”

Six days later he was still asking. “If we choose to start early they are not daily waivers right, they would still be weekly?” Then the line that should have settled the procedural argument by itself: “There was 4 different options the other day.” And the entirely reasonable request that nobody met: “They choices should be posted now so we can sit on it and decide when the 8th comes.”

THE BALLOT GREW — An off-calendar vote does something predictable. It invites every other idea in. By August 4, with the waiver question still unsettled, Still The Creamiest had followed the precedent to its logical end: “Are we voting on all things? Adding an additional roster spot to 20 Or Adding an additional IR spot to 3.” His justification was hard to argue with — “Why not it's talked about every year” — and he was right that they are raised annually and dropped annually.

The Pork Chop Express, who had called the vote in the first place, declined on exactly the grounds he had already stepped over: “Additional IR spot totally makes sense. But I'm not fighting for another vote not on our official voting day.” By the morning of the vote itself the Powers of Pain was proposing a ban on kickers on the grounds of their average age, under the only precedent the fortnight had established: “It's still August 8th. Another vote!”

THE CORRECTION — Then the case fell apart, and it was pulled apart by the man arguing for it. The Machines, who had authored the daily-waivers plan and voted to open the wire, went back through the calendar and found the premise was wrong. Waivers had never been scheduled for September 2. On a normal year — draft on August 23 — they would have run on August 26. The gap the whole freeze was built to solve was three weeks, not five.

He posted the correction himself, against his own side, and explained why: “We don't want to be accused of voter fraud by presenting incorrect information down the line.” Then he reissued the poll with the true dates on it. It is the single most creditable thing anybody did in the whole affair, and it decided the vote.

THE VOTE — August 8. The Pork Chop Express opened the floor at ten to six in the morning — “Vote Day! I will put the vote up on this chat. Please just vote.” — and asked that argument be taken to the other chat so the poll would not get buried. It got buried anyway.

The corrected ballot gave two options: open the wire that week, on August 13, or open it when it would have opened normally, on August 26. The count finished 9-6 for waiting. By late morning it was already out of reach. “It's over. Already 8 votes for no,” the Express announced, and asked the New World Order to set waivers for the 26th.

THE CAMPAIGN — For a vote that changed nothing, it was contested like a swing state. The Beaver Eaters, watching the poll stay open, offered the only genuinely new proposal of the day: “Since the poll is still open my vote can be bought.” The Hairy Gumbas suggested the count was closer than it looked and that “the machines official voting machine or mail in ballot was hacked,” which was at least thematically consistent, and The Machines himself conceded that “I guess you really can't trust the voting machines” before announcing he was checking out because it was his anniversary.

THE VERDICT — The Smoke Dragons, who had spent two weeks arguing that the process was the problem, collected on it in one line: “If only someone could have foreseen the chaos of having half ass votes whenever anyone wants to change something.”

The Machines, on the losing side of a vote he had corrected the ballot for, took it better than anyone had a right to expect. “It's the power of democracy,” he wrote. “I respect the ruling and the vote.” He also spent the following week asking anybody who would listen when the waivers actually were, which is its own kind of commentary.

The Horse Collars have not reconciled. A week after the vote he was still making the case, and it is a decent one: “Exactly why I am against the delay. Diminishes the ability to look at the draft and then efficiently utilize waivers and FA to both make calculated risks and fill out the roster.”

WHERE IT LANDS — On August 19, with the argument eleven days cold, the New World Order asked whether there was an official date yet and then answered his own question: “So waivers open on the 25th then and clear on the 26th.” That is four days from now.

So the league moved its draft a month early, froze the wire for a fortnight, held a vote, and put waivers back exactly where the calendar had them. The thing that did change is harder to see on a schedule. For two weeks this league could not reliably say what it was voting on, and the man who only ever asked for the options to be written down got his answer in the end: they are written down on draft day. That is what the Smoke Dragons had been saying since the first afternoon, and it is the only argument from the whole affair that won.

Sourcing: reconstructed from the league chats, July 24 to August 19, 2026. Every quotation is verbatim and machine-checked against the corpus by scripts/verify_quotes.py before publication. Vote totals are the corrected poll as it stands in the record: 6 to open August 13, 9 to open August 26. The chat itself is not in this repository and never will be.

investigations.headline: Four Divisions, Two Conferences, One Belt
investigations.subhead: The desk calls every round of it, and says what would make each call look silly.
paragraphs: Every pick below comes off the same three things: what a team scored last season, what the Powers of Pain made of its draft, and what the franchise has done when it got to January before. Records are the worst of the three — this league just watched a 7-7 team win the whole thing — so points carry more weight here than wins do.
THE CARD — Four division winners, four wild cards, two conference champions, one belt. Here is the desk's call on all of it, and the reasoning underneath, so it can be held against us in January.
JOHN MCCLANE CONFERENCE — Two divisions, two wild cards, and one of these four teams reaches the final.

SPARTAN — The Machines. Went 9-5 on 1,417 points, the most in the division, off the only top-eight finish in every season the records hold. The Chops own him head to head and it has never once cost him a season. A B+ class on top of the deepest roster in the league. This is the safest of the four calls.

SPECTRE SYNDICATE — Guido Haters. Taking the division off the reigning champion, which needs saying out loud. The Powers of Pain won the title on 1,183 points — fewer than any team in the bracket — while the Haters posted 1,275 on the identical 7-7 record. Same wins, ninety-two more points, and a B draft against a champion who does not grade himself. The title was real. The scoring underneath it was not.

JOHN MCCLANE WILD CARDS — Powers of Pain and Lil' Chops. The champion as a wild card is not an insult, it is arithmetic: 1,183 points does not win a division containing a team that scored ninety-two more. He gets in anyway, because three titles from four title games is a manager who knows the three weeks that count. The Chops take the second on 1,331 points and a series lead over the team picked to win the conference.
COBRA KAI CONFERENCE — Two divisions, two wild cards, and one of these four teams reaches the final.

BLACK AND BLUE — Big Blue. The hardest division to call and the one most likely to embarrass this desk. The Express scored 1,531 to Big Blue's 1,490 off the same 11-3 record. The separator is the summer: an A class against a C+, and a franchise that has been to three title games and lost none of them. The Beaver Eaters scored 1,466 and missed the bracket from here last year, which tells you what this division does to good teams.

THE FOUR HORSEMEN — New World Order. Horse Collars won it at 10-4 and are not being picked to repeat it, because they scored fewer points than the team behind them and then drafted C-, second worst on the board. The New World Order put up 1,358, the most in the division, took a B class, and have twelve top-eight finishes in eighteen seasons. Last year's eighth was the outlier, not the level.

COBRA KAI WILD CARDS — Pork Chop Express and Horse Collars. The Express miss the division and are still the highest-scoring team in this league at 1,531. That is the Black and Blue tax. Horse Collars take the last place on 10-4 and a division title already banked, which leaves the Beaver Eaters at 1,466 points on the outside again.

JOHN MCCLANE CHAMPION — The Machines. Nobody in this conference has his record and nobody is close. 192-47 across eighteen seasons, eleven title games, and a bracket that has never once been played without him. Getting to the final is the thing he does.

COBRA KAI CHAMPION — Big Blue. Through the Express, who beat him to the points title and lost the game that mattered, and through a New World Order side that has reached four finals and won one. Big Blue is three-for-three in title games. The road to one is the part he has to prove again.
THE CHAMPION — Big Blue. So: Big Blue over The Machines, and this desk is aware of how that sounds after picking the Machines to walk his conference.

Here is the whole argument, and it is not the trophy count — across the full life of this league the Machines, Big Blue and the Powers of Pain all have four championships and nobody has a fifth. It is what happens once they get there. In the eighteen seasons on record the Machines have played eleven title games and won four: 4-7 on the last Sunday. Big Blue has played three and won three. 3-0.

That is a small sample and this desk knows it. Seven losses across eighteen years is not a flaw in a manager, it is what happens to anyone who keeps arriving, and it is the reason he has as many belts as anyone. But a pick has to come down on one side of something, and the only place these two separate is the week the season ends.

WHAT WOULD MAKE THIS LOOK STUPID — Four things, in order of likelihood. Still The Cream drew an A+, the best class anybody got, and finished sixteenth: if that draft lands, the Spectre Syndicate pick is wrong twice over. The Killer Klowns took an A- and have already won a title inside the last two years. The Hairy Gumbas hold the reigning champion 18-6 and nobody has picked them for anything. And the Beaver Eaters scored 1,466 points last season, more than three of the four teams picked to win divisions, and are picked for nothing at all.

Sourcing: 2025 finishes, points and career totals from the league record, the same eighteen seasons used everywhere else in this issue. Draft grades from the Powers of Pain's 2026 board. Head-to-head from the 2,344 games behind The Grudge Report. Every number is interpolated from those files by scripts/build_picks.py; the opinions are the desk's own and carry no such guarantee.

investigations.headline: All Sixteen, Division by Division
investigations.subhead: Where every team finished, what the draft gave them, and why the division you are in decides more of your season than anything you do in it.
paragraphs: Sixteen teams, two conferences, four divisions. Six of your fourteen games are against the three teams you are about to read alongside, which means the division you are in is the single biggest fact about your season — bigger than your draft, bigger than your roster, and entirely outside your control. Win it and you are seeded above every wild card in your conference no matter what anybody's record says. Here is all sixteen, in the order they finished.
JOHN MCCLANE CONFERENCE — Two divisions, four places: the two division winners, and two wild cards for whoever is left.
SPARTAN — One franchise has finished top eight in every season on record, and the other three are playing for the one wild card he does not take. 225 points separate top from bottom.

LIL' CHOPS — Went 7-7 on 1,331 points and finished sixth, which undersells the most interesting fact about them. They hold a 6-3 record against The Machines — the only winning series anyone has against him — and across those nine games the cumulative points difference is four. Not four a game. Four in total. The Powers of Pain gave the draft a B- for a single running back, which is either discipline or a quiet year, and the Chops have been quiet before.

THE MACHINES — Went 9-5 on 1,417 points and finished seventh. None of which is the story. The story is 192-47 across the eighteen seasons on record, four championships, eleven title games, and a top-eight finish in every single year the records hold — no other franchise has more than twelve. He beats Still The Cream 30-4. He beats the Killer Klowns 26-1. Exactly one team in this league has a winning record against him, and they are sitting directly above him in this division. The one crack: seventh place two years running, and no belt since 2018. A B+ draft says he is not planning to make that three.

MASTER-JETI — Went 7-7 on 1,298 points and finished tenth, a year after three straight seasons inside the top six. There is a championship on the shelf and six top-eight finishes in fourteen seasons here, so the floor is real. He did not appear on the Powers of Pain's board this summer, which in a league that grades everything is its own kind of statement.

KILLER KLOWNS — Won the championship in 2024 and finished fourteenth in 2025 at 3-11. Defending champions have gone over the side before — twice to fifteenth — so the fall is not unheard of, only steep. 1,192 points is the least in the division, and the franchise carries a 1-26 record against The Machines that is not a typo. The reason to watch anyway: the Powers of Pain graded this draft A-, the fourth-best mark on the board, and a team that has already proved it can win the whole thing does not need to be good for long.
SPECTRE SYNDICATE — The champion lives here, and so does the worst points total of any division winner's neighbourhood. Nobody in it scored 1,300. 272 points separate top from bottom.

POWERS OF PAIN — The champion. 7-7, 1,183 points — fewer than any other team that made the bracket — and the belt. Read the four years before it in order: fifteenth, eleventh, tenth, tenth, and then first. There are three titles here in the seasons on record and four title games, so this is a franchise that knows the walk. The thing standing in the way of a repeat is not the Machines and it is not the Express. It is the Hairy Gumbas, who hold a 18-6 record over him across 24 games and are not in his division, which is the only mercy in it.

GUIDO HATERS — Went 7-7 on 1,275 points and finished fourth, the most points in the division and nothing much to show for it. The last five finishes read thirteenth, third, thirteenth, thirteenth, fourth, which is not a trend, it is a coin. The long story here is the quietest series in the league: 45 games against the Powers of Pain, sitting 21-24, two divisional rivals who have almost never said a word about it. A B draft. He is closer than the finishes suggest.

SMOKE DRAGONS — Went 5-9 on 1,003 points and finished thirteenth — the fewest points in the division and the second fewest in the league. In eighteen seasons on record there are no championships and, harder to look at, no title games. Not lost — reached. The Machines have him 3-18. The C+ draft leaned on a receiver and a developmental quarterback, which is a plan that needs two years, and the Dragons have had plenty of those.

STILL THE CREAM — Finished sixteenth at 2-12 on 1,028 points, and then watched the rename go to somebody else on the tiebreak. 97-142 across eighteen seasons with no titles and no finals is the hardest line in this preview. So is 4-30 against The Machines. And yet: the Powers of Pain handed this draft an A+, the best grade given to anybody all summer. Last place has the first pick and the best class in the league. If it does not turn now, it does not turn.
COBRA KAI CONFERENCE — Two divisions, four places: the two division winners, and two wild cards for whoever is left.

BLACK AND BLUE — Three of the four highest-scoring teams in the league, in one division, playing each other twice. Somebody very good misses the playoffs out of this. 252 points separate top from bottom.

PORK CHOP EXPRESS — Scored 1,531 points, more than anyone in this league, went 11-3, and lost the final. Finished second. That is a season most managers would take and nobody wants to repeat. The worry is the summer: a C+ class described as depth rather than difference, in a division where the other three all scored 1,466 or better. Being the best offence in the league did not settle 2025 and it will not settle this one either.

BIG BLUE — Went 11-3 on 1,490 points and finished fifth. The résumé is four championships, level with anyone who has ever played here, and inside the eighteen seasons on record three title games and three wins — the only unbeaten record in the building — off 144-95 overall. The last two years read fourth and fifth, which for this franchise counts as a slump. He drew an A for the draft and holds Wookie Leaks 19-6. The reason to be careful about writing him off: he has reached three finals and never lost one.

BEAVER EATERS — Here is the cruellest line in the preview. 144-95 across eighteen seasons — identical, win for win and loss for loss, to Big Blue's — and no championships in those seasons to Big Blue's four. In 2025 he scored 1,466 points, third most in the league, went 7-7, and finished ninth: outside the bracket entirely. Then the Powers of Pain graded the draft a D, the only one on the board, and called two of the three picks baffling. Historically one of the best drafters in this league. Not this year.

WOOKIE LEAKS — Went 7-7 on 1,279 points and finished eleventh, the fewest points in a division where everybody else cleared 1,460. Big Blue has him 6-19 across 25 games and The Machines 3-17, so the schedule is not doing him any favours. The summer was the good news: an A draft built on a receiver who fell further than he should have, and two swings at a thin running back class. If the receiver stays healthy this is a different team. If.
THE FOUR HORSEMEN — The widest division in the league, and the one carrying the rename. 537 points separate top from bottom.

HORSE COLLARS — Went 10-4 on 1,343 points and finished third, up from eleventh and twelfth the two years before it. There is a championship here and ten top-eight finishes in eighteen seasons, so the jump is a return rather than a surprise. The summer is the argument against: a C-, second worst on the board, for a draft the Powers of Pain described as laying up. His longest series is 41 games against the New World Order, sitting 18-23, and he sees them twice a year.

NEW WORLD ORDER — Went 9-5 on 1,358 points and finished eighth, the most points in the division. This is the most consistently dangerous franchise nobody calls dangerous: four title games, twelve top-eight finishes in eighteen seasons, and finishes of fifth, second, third and second before last year's eighth. The B draft took two first-round receivers and left the roster lopsided, which the Powers of Pain flagged and the standings may not care about.

HAIRY GUMBAS — Went 8-6 on 1,221 points and finished twelfth, and the record does something strange with this franchise. He has four top-eight finishes in eighteen seasons, the fewest of anyone here, and no championships from two title games. And yet he owns the reigning champion 18-6 across 24 games. The C draft took a quarterback who needs three years behind a starter, on a roster whose best players do not have three years. That tension is the whole season.

HEAVY HITTERS — Finished fifteenth at 2-12 on 821 points — 182 behind the next-lowest team in the league, a margin that is difficult to look at. The rename is his. What the standings do not say: there is a championship on this shelf, and a 16-10 record over the Jet-I across 26 games. The Powers of Pain gave the draft a B+, fifth best on the board, built around the one back everybody agreed was elite. New name, first pick, best class in the division. Worse hands have been dealt.

ACROSS THE LEAGUE — The highest-scoring team of 2025 was Pork Chop Express on 1531; the lowest was Heavy Hitters on 821. That is a gap of 710 points between the top and the bottom of this league, which is roughly a touchdown and a half every week for a whole season. The team at the top of it lost the final. The team at the bottom of it is getting a new name.

investigations.headline: The Champion Who Lost More Than He Won
investigations.subhead: The Powers of Pain won the 2025 title at 7-7 with the fewest points of any team in the field. The format left the door open. He walked through it.
paragraphs: Here is the 2025 season in one line. The Powers of Pain finished 7-7. He scored 1,183 points, fewer than any other team that made the playoffs and fewer than four teams that missed. He is the champion.
None of that is a scandal, and none of it is an accident. It is the format doing exactly what the format was built to do, and it is worth understanding before anybody sets a lineup this year.

HOW IT HAPPENS — Eight teams qualify: the four division winners, plus two wild cards from each conference. Win your division and you are in, and you are seeded above every wild card no matter what the record says. The Powers of Pain came out of the Spectre Syndicate at 7-7, from a division where the Guido Haters also finished 7-7 and Still The Cream finished 2-12. Somebody had to come out of it.
What the format rewards is not being the best team in the league across fourteen weeks. It is being the best team in three particular ones.
He was. That is the whole point of a postseason, and anyone who wants to be sour about it should look at the 2024 champion, the Killer Klowns, who won the whole thing at 6-8.
WHAT IT MEANS FOR 2026 — Two things, and they pull in opposite directions.

The first is that a division title is worth more in this league than in almost any comparable format. It is not a tiebreaker or a banner — it is a seed, and the seed is the whole tournament. Four of the sixteen teams in this league will get in on a technicality this year. Do not spend December scoreboard-watching for a wild card if you can simply win four games in your own division.

The second is that the Powers of Pain has to do it again from a harder position. He is no longer the surprise. He has the trophy, he has the target, and he is in a division with the Guido Haters, who matched his record last year, and a Still The Cream side that just drew the best draft grade in the league.

THE RECORD SAYS — This is a franchise that knows how to be there. In the eighteen seasons this desk holds records for, the Powers of Pain has reached four title games and won three of them — the best conversion rate of any manager who has been to more than one. The Machines has eleven finals in the same span and four belts. Across the full life of the league, though, the honours run level three ways: the Powers of Pain, The Machines and Big Blue have four championships each, and nobody has a fifth.
He does not get there often. He wins when he does.

investigations.headline: Two Wins, Eight Hundred and Twenty-One Points, One New Name
investigations.subhead: The Heavy Hitters and Still The Cream both finished 2-12. The tiebreaker went to points, and the Hitters lost it by a distance that is difficult to look at.
paragraphs: The oldest rule in this league is also the only punishment in it that outlives the season. Finish last and you are renamed for the following year, and the league votes on what you get called.
The 2025 race for it came down to two teams and did not resolve until the points were counted.

THE TIEBREAK — The Heavy Hitters finished 2-12. Still The Cream finished 2-12. Level on the only number that usually matters, the question went to points scored, and it was not close: the Hitters put up 821, the Cream 1,028.

That 821 is the number to sit with. The next-worst total in the league was 1,003 — the Smoke Dragons, who at least had five wins to show for it. The Heavy Hitters were 182 points adrift of fifteenth place. Across a fourteen-game season that is thirteen points a week, every week, of daylight between them and the second-worst offence in the SCFL.
So the name change is theirs.

THE CRUEL PART — The Hitters did not have a bad draft. The Powers of Pain graded their 2026 class a B+, tied for the fifth-best mark on a board of fourteen — level with the Machines, and ahead of the Express, the Gumbas and the Collars.

The cruel part is who they finished level with. Still The Cream also went 2-12 — and drew an A+, the best grade POP handed out all summer. Two teams tied at the bottom, one walks away with the best draft class in the league and his name intact, and the other takes the rename with a perfectly respectable haul.
That is the rule working as designed. It is not meant to be fair. It is meant to be memorable.

WHAT COMES NEXT — The league votes. History says the vote is not kind and the name is not chosen to flatter — the SCFL has been doing this for the better part of twenty years, and the archive is full of franchises who spent a season answering to something they would not repeat in front of their children.
The consolation, such as it is, arrives in the spring: last place takes the 1.01. As The Machines once put it, getting the number one pick helps a little.
It has helped before. It is not helping the Heavy Hitters get their name back.

investigations.headline: Everything Good Is in One Division
investigations.subhead: The three highest-scoring teams in the SCFL last season all play in Black and Blue. Two of them went 11-3. They have to keep playing each other.
paragraphs: Sort last season's sixteen teams by points scored and stop at three. The Pork Chop Express, 1,531. Big Blue, 1,490. The Beaver Eaters, 1,466.
All three are in Black and Blue. They play each other twice a year.

THE MATH OF IT — Six games a season are divisional, which means a Black and Blue team spends nearly half its schedule against the best-scoring group in the league. The Express and Big Blue both finished 11-3, the two best records in the SCFL, and they did it while beating each other up.

The Beaver Eaters are the exhibit. They scored the third-most points in the league — more than the eventual champion by 283 — and finished 7-7. On any other schedule that is a comfortable playoff team. In Black and Blue it was ninth in the final table and no playoff berth at all.
AND THE FOURTH TEAM — Wookie Leaks also went 7-7 in there, which in the circumstances is a good deal better than it looks, and he has drawn an A for his 2026 draft. So has Big Blue.
Which is the genuinely alarming part for the rest of the league. The division that already had the three best offences just added two of the three best draft classes.

THE STAKES — Only one of these four wins the division, and the seed that comes with it. The other three are fighting for two Cobra Kai wild cards against a Four Horsemen field that includes Horse Collars at 10-4 and the New World Order at 9-5.
Somebody very good is going to miss the playoffs out of this division. Possibly two somebodies.

It is also the division with the most recent history of settling things properly. Big Blue and the Beaver Eaters have met six times in the postseason — second only to Big Blue and The Machines — and the Beavers have taken four of the six despite trailing the all-time series 10-15.
That is the shape of Black and Blue. Enormous scoring, no room, and a postseason record of the bigger name losing.

investigations.headline: The Grudge Report
investigations.subhead: Twenty-one franchises, 2,344 games, eighteen seasons of matchups. Who actually has a rivalry in this league, who has a tormentor, and which of the great grudges turn out to be invented.
investigations.byline: The SCFL NewsRoom · The Record Room
paragraphs: This league has always described itself in grudges. Ask any manager who his rival is and you will get an answer in under a second, delivered with total confidence and no evidence whatsoever.

So the Newsroom went and counted. Every matchup in the league's records — eighteen seasons, twenty-one franchises, 2,344 games — reconciled against the standings until the two agreed exactly. Then we counted something else: who actually talks to whom, and how often it stops being friendly.
The results do not flatter everybody, and one of the things they did was demolish a couple of the stories this desk was ready to print.

THE METHOD — A rivalry needs three things, and this desk scored all three. You have to play each other a lot. The series has to be close enough to be worth arguing about. And you have to actually engage — measured as back-and-forth in the chat, normalised so the quiet managers aren't punished for being quiet and the loud ones don't win on volume.

Two facts about how this league is built had to be respected, and ignoring either one produces nonsense. The first is the schedule. Sixteen teams, two conferences, two divisions of four. You play your own division twice — six games — the other division in your conference once, and four more scattered across the other conference to fill the card. Which means the size of a head-to-head sample is mostly a fact about the schedule rather than about the two men involved: share a division for a decade and you will pile up thirty games without either of you choosing it. Shared history here is counted in seasons spent in the same division, not in raw games.

The second is the postseason. Eight teams qualify — the four division winners plus two wild cards from each conference — and then all sixteen keep playing for three more weeks, the bottom half in a consolation ladder that decides nothing. The records flag every one of those as a playoff game. They are not. A playoff meeting in this report means both teams qualified. That is twelve games a season, not twenty-four, and sorting it properly is what killed two of the rivalries this desk was ready to print.

Note also what is deliberately absent. We counted how often exchanges turn sharp, because that says something about a pairing. We are not printing what was said. This league has been friends for thirty years, and the worst thing anyone typed at eleven o'clock on a Sunday night is not evidence of anything except a bad week.
THE TORMENTOR — Start with the finding that reorganises everything else. The Machines does not have a rivalry with most of this league. He has victims.
Against the Killer Klowns he is 26-1. Against Still The Creamiest, 30-4. Against the Smoke Dragons, 18-3. Against the Hairy Gumbas, 17-3. Against Wookie Leaks, 17-3. Against the Beaver Eaters, 10-2.

That is six franchises and 134 games at a combined 118-16, with a points margin north of four thousand. The loudest arguments in this league are not between equals — they are the sound of six men losing to the same person for the better part of two decades.
It holds up in the postseason too, where it counts. He has met the Smoke Dragons five times in the playoffs and won all five.

THE RECORD — And to be clear about what that adds up to, because the standings deserve the credit: The Machines has won four championships, a total matched by the Powers of Pain and by Big Blue and beaten by nobody. What separates him is the arriving. He has played in eleven of the eighteen title games in the records this desk holds, which is not a statistic about luck. It means that in more than half the seasons we can account for, he was the last or second-to-last man standing.

He has lost seven of those eleven. That is the line people reach for, and it is worth being careful with. A man who reaches the final eleven times is going to lose finals; the seven managers who beat him were each having the best season of their lives, and a fantasy final is one week of scoring in which the better team loses all the time. The Machines has as many belts as anyone and more finals than anyone by a distance of seven. Those are the facts in the right order.
THE BEST RIVALRY IN THE LEAGUE — Which brings us to the one pairing that has everything, and it is not close.

The Machines and Big Blue have met seven times in the playoffs — more than any other pair of franchises in league history — and Big Blue has won four of the seven. The regular-season series belongs to The Machines at 16-13 across twenty-nine games, which is exactly the shape a real rivalry should have: one man edges the long haul, the other takes the games that matter.

In 2023 Big Blue beat him in the final, 125.5 to 100. It was the middle jewel of a three-peat — 2021, 2022, 2023 — and it makes Big Blue three-for-three in title games, the only perfect record in the building. He has also won the last five meetings between them outright.
One man is 118-16 against six franchises. Against the seventh he is 3-4 when it counts. That is a rivalry, and it is the only one he has.
THE PUREST — If you want the pairing that behaves most like a rivalry is supposed to, it is the Pork Chop Express and the Smoke Dragons.

The series is 9-7 across sixteen games, a margin of 154 points over nine seasons — close enough that either man can claim it depending on the day. What separates it is the engagement: 21.6% of all the back-and-forth these two have in the chat is with each other.

Only one pairing engages more, and it proves the point rather than spoiling it. The Machines and the Smoke Dragons run at 23.4% — the highest mutual figure in the SCFL — and that series is 18-3. Men talk most at the person beating them. Set aside the pairings where somebody is simply losing, and the Express and the Dragons are the most engaged evenly-matched teams in the building, by a distance.

THE OLD MARRIAGES — The longest series in league history belongs to two men nobody thinks of as rivals at all: the Powers of Pain and the Guido Haters have played forty-five times, splitting them 24-21, with four postseason meetings on top. And it is not an accident — they have been divisional rivals in sixteen of their eighteen seasons together, which is the longest continuous division pairing in the league. Two men scheduled against each other twice a year for the better part of two decades, and almost nothing said about any of it.

Close behind: the New World Order and Horse Collars, 41 games and sixteen shared divisional seasons; the New World Order and the Beaver Eaters, 37 games and a series standing at 19-18 — one game apart after seventeen seasons together, five of their meetings in the playoffs. And Horse Collars and the Beaver Eaters, 35 games, thirteen of them divisional years, 19-16 to the Beavers.
These are the old marriages of the SCFL. Enormous shared history, almost no heat, and a scoreline that refuses to separate.

THE POSTSEASON SPECIALISTS — One franchise has quietly made a habit of ending Big Blue's Januarys. The Beaver Eaters have met him six times in the playoffs — second only to The Machines–Big Blue file — and have taken four of the six, despite trailing the overall series 10-15.
That is the postseason inverting a regular-season order, which is the rarest thing in these records and the only honest version of a giant-killing in the league.
THE ONES THAT WEREN'T THERE — Two rivalries this desk fully expected to write did not survive the counting, and they are worth reporting as corrections rather than quietly dropping.

The Heavy Hitters and Still The Creamiest look, at first glance, like the great unspoken feud: twenty-seven games and a series sitting at 14-13. Sort the postseason properly and they have met four times, and split them 2-2. The Hairy Gumbas and the Heavy Hitters, who appeared to have a postseason stranglehold, have never met in a playoff game at all. Every one of those meetings was in the consolation bracket, which is to say none of them were playing for anything.

There is a lesson in that for everybody who tells rivalry stories, this desk very much included. Half the grudges in a fantasy league are two teams who kept running into each other in week fifteen while both seasons were already over.
THE QUIET ONES — Two pairings deserve mention precisely because nobody argues about them.
The Jet-I and the Smoke Dragons have played twenty-nine times and the series sits at 15-14. Dead level across a decade and a half, and it has never once become a talking point.

And the tightest series in the entire dataset, by the only measure that cannot be argued with: Lamb Chops versus The Machines. Nine games, and a cumulative points difference of four. Not four a game — four in total, with Lamb Chops holding a 6-3 edge. The newest manager in the league and the most decorated, separated by a rounding error, and neither of them has ever mentioned it.

THE HALF-POINT GAMES — Two playoff games in league history have been decided by half a point: the Killer Klowns over the Jet-I in 2024, and Big Blue over the Pork Chop Express in 2018. Somewhere in each of those weeks a man set a lineup on a Sunday morning and never learned how close it came.
THE VERDICT — The league's own account of itself turns out to be about half right.

The rivalries people talk about loudest are mostly real, and the Express and the Dragons are exactly as advertised. The best of them all is The Machines and Big Blue, which has the games, the stakes, the title and the current streak. But the most remarkable series in the book — forty-five games between the Powers of Pain and the Guido Haters — belongs to two men who have never made a noise about it, and two of the feuds this desk believed in turned out to be consolation football.

Sourcing: 2,344 head-to-head games from the league's own records, 2008–2025, reconciled against the stored standings for every team-season. A playoff meeting means both teams finished in the top eight; consolation-bracket games are excluded, and every season's title game was checked against the champion the records already name. Where the source rounds scores to the half point, results were recovered from the standings; one game in the entire dataset is a genuine tie. Engagement figures are aggregate counts from the league chat — no message text was used or reproduced. The full board is in the app under The Record Room.

investigations.headline: The Roll Call
investigations.subhead: Tony Romo. Leonard Fournette. Kareem Hunt. Kyler Murray. Cooper Kupp. DK Metcalf. And, as of last Thursday, Jordyn Tyson. A field guide to the SCFL's only working curse.
paragraphs: Every league has superstitions. Most of them are noise — a lucky jersey, a bad seat, a manager who will not say a player's name out loud in a good week. The SCFL has exactly one that keeps surviving contact with the evidence, and it can be stated in six words.
Players the Wookie trades away get hurt.

Not while he owns them. That is the part people get wrong when they first arrive. On his roster they are fine — bored, maybe, occasionally underused, but structurally intact. It is the leaving that does it. The moment a player crosses out of the Wookie's building and into somebody else's, the clock starts. And the clock has a very good record.

It has a symbol, too. 🥶 — the cold face. In this league it is not a temperature. It is a mark, and when the Wookie posts it, the chat goes quiet for a second and then starts writing the obituary. Horse Collars gave the whole thing its formal name in October 2022, watching it work in real time: “Voodoo for trades. Wookie Curse. He has the curse.”

Nobody voted it into existence and nobody wrote it down. The closest thing to a founding document is a throwaway line from August 1, 2021, when an argument about something else entirely pulled the Wookie into a thread he had slept through. “I think I used those for the curse,” he wrote. “Only time I think I really even mentioned voodoo in here was for the 🥶.”
That is the whole liturgy. No ritual, no doll, no incantation. A man, an emoji, and a transaction log that keeps ending in an injury report.
What follows is the roll call. It is not complete. It is only the ones the chat caught.

TONY ROMO — Patient zero, and the case the Wookie himself still nominates. Pressed in February 2022 on whether the thing was even still live, he answered like a man reciting scripture: “Romo was still the greatest instance of the 🥶 ever.” Then, because he is not a monster, an apology to the manager who had been holding the receipt: “Sorry @Mike.”

The mechanism, in his own words: “Traded and less than a week later broken back.” The Machines, who keeps this league's institutional memory the way other men keep receipts, offered no rebuttal at all. He offered corroboration: “It was next level.”

LEONARD FOURNETTE — The only name on this list who was marked out loud, in public, before anything happened to him. On a Thursday night in September 2021, watching from across the league, the Wookie posted four characters and a name: “🥶 Fournette….”

Fournette came onto the Wookie's roster in the enormous August 2022 quarterback chain and was moved along again inside the year. By November 13 the Wookie was noting the aftermath in the chat himself, in four words: “Lenny hip injury too.”

KAREEM HUNT — This one is not our finding. It belongs to the Pork Chop Express, who spent his rookie year in this league acquiring players out of the Wookie's building and has never fully recovered from the experience. His confession, filed in October 2022, is quoted in full because it cannot be improved on:
“Wookie had Fournette and Hunt. Lenny came to me in the Cousins trade I believe. Hunt in the Carr trade. I said the curse didn't exist. Hunt kicked a women on camera.”

ZACK MOSS — The case that established the curse travels through paper as well as flesh. Horse Collars, sifting the wreckage of assets acquired from the Wookie, noted that “that occurred with my other pick I got from you. Moss.” The reply was not a denial. It was an apology, and a faintly alarmed one: “Shit. My bad, Doc. Lol. Didn't realize it extended to picks of mine too.”
Horse Collars asked the only question that mattered — why would it not, and had anybody ever studied this thing for validity?

KYLER MURRAY — The loudest one, and the one that suggests you do not even have to stay long. In the August 2022 blockbuster Murray came into the Wookie's building from The Machines and went straight back out the other side to the Smoke Dragons. He barely touched the carpet.

On the night of December 12, on a play nobody touched him on either, he did not get up. The chat has all of it in real time. “Murray. Oh no,” from the Pork Chop Express. “Non contact.” Then: “He's done.” Then: “He went down like a sack of potatoes.”

And from the man who had taken him four months earlier, the line that belongs on the plaque: “I had the week locked up. Should have kept him on the bench and avoided injury.” Two minutes later, all of it: “Very upsetting.”

COOPER KUPP — Left for The Machines on September 13, 2023, in perfect working order, for a future first and a receiver. He lasted about six weeks. On November 19 Horse Collars filed the two-word update the league had been waiting on without admitting it was waiting: “Kupp hurt.” Eleven days after that, The Machines was explaining his own receiver to the room: “Stafford was out and now he's dealing with an ankle. Injuries always a concern with Kupp.”

DK METCALF — As late as July 24, 2024, The Machines was citing Metcalf as evidence that the Wookie's roster was young and healthy: “Wookie has Swift, Richardson, Metcalf, Williams — not like his team is old.” Metcalf moved to The Machines inside that same season. On October 20 he was carted off. The buyer's account, live: “Metcalf grabbed bunch of points first thankfully. But carted out.” And then the sentence every trade partner of the Wookie eventually types: “Just can't keep this f***ing team healthy for one week.”
JORDYN TYSON — The newest name, and the one that came within a day of the record.

On August 6 the Wookie sent Tyson to the New World Order. The chat spent that evening doing what this chat does, which is arguing about it at length. On August 13, in a joint practice against Jacksonville, Tyson pulled up holding a hamstring. The reporting has him out something like two months, with a live chance it eats into the regular season. One outlet used the word bleak.
Seven days. Romo went in less than a week.

The Powers of Pain, who had graded the Wookie's rookie class a few weeks earlier, may want to check whether he owns a crystal ball as well as a curse. His write-up flagged the same worry twice in a single paragraph: “If Tyson can stay healthy he has the talent to create a 1A/1B situation in New Orleans with Chris Olave.” And: he “drew Stefan Diggs comparisons, which is exciting if he can just remain healthy.”

ARE YOU A VICTIM OF THE WOOKIE CURSE? — You are not alone. If a player has torn, pulled, broken, retired or been carted off within days of arriving on your roster from the Wookie, help is available. Reach the SCFL NewsRoom on WhatsApp. Counselors are standing by.

THE DOCTRINE — What elevates all this above a running joke is that the league treats the mark as permanent, and as a property of the player rather than the moment. In February 2022 The Machines waved off an injury worry about somebody else with a sentence that reads like case law: “He was never a wookie, so at least the SCFL boogie man hasn't touched him.”
Once a Wookie, always eligible. Nobody has ever been de-listed.
THE OWNER — He has never denied any of it. He has leaned all the way in.

In December 2021 he announced a procurement — “hopefully my Hurts voodoo doll gets here soon 🤞🏻” — then talked himself out of his own scheme two lines later: “But I never had Hurts, so the curse won't be in play.” Even the owner respects the eligibility rules.

In September 2022 he traded Matt Ryan away, took some chat abuse for it, and pointed the thing at a manager who had just tried to embarrass him in public: “It's all good, Dave. I hope Ryan breaks both clavicles. See what Foles has left in the tank.” A beat later came the slogan he has been running on ever since — “Make the Curse Great Again” — and a beat after that: “Should've hashtagged that.”

By December 2025 he had stopped bothering with players altogether and gone straight at a rival's season: “Already got Schechter the f*** outta the playoffs, let's see if the old 🥶 is back, just in another form.”

He was joking. He is always joking. Nobody in this league has ever been entirely sure how much — which is the whole appeal, and also the reason The Machines has twice gone looking for a connection to explain an unrelated bad month. In December 2022: “Did wookie ever own Jimmy g!” And, immediately after: “Wondering if the curse is still active.” In October of that year, extending the doctrine to an entire position group, “a strange Wookie-style curse on potential Jets QBs they will face.”

Nobody laughs it off. In this league, laughing it off is documented as the thing that makes it worse. Horse Collars watched somebody try it once and reported the result in two lines: they “laughed off the curse 🥶,” and then “it came alive with vengeance.”

THE CHAT REOPENS THE FILE — This desk did not have to go looking for the reaction. On the evening of August 17, as the Tyson news filtered through, Lil Chops got there first: “Wookie’s voodoo doll came thru lol.” The Machines, who has spent five years treating this as an open question, asked it again: “Wait — is the Wookie curse back?”
The Wookie answered with a single character. 🥶

Then he did what he always does, which is claim the history rather than deny it. “Tony Romo is still #1 Wookie curse that has ever descended upon the SCFL,” he wrote, and then: “Yes. Can’t deny that curse in all its glory.”

And the Pork Chop Express — the man who has bought more of these players than anybody and who owns the one comparable disaster in league history — drew the line between his own record and the Wookie’s: “PCE only has Luck as a booby trap. The Wookie curse runs deep. It’s been dormant for a while. But if it’s back, there’s some owners who are in trouble.”

THE WIRE OPENS ON THE 26TH — The Wookie will pick up the phone. He is one of the most active traders in the league, he answers everybody, and he is generally reasonable on price. Somewhere in the middle of that conversation you will realise you are about to acquire a perfectly healthy football player from a man whose last several perfectly healthy football players are currently listed as questionable, doubtful, out, or retired.
Take the trade. Everyone does. Just don't say you weren't warned, don't say it out loud afterwards, and whatever else you do — do not laugh it off.

Sourcing: chat quotations verified verbatim against the SCFL league chat (286,903 messages, May 2021 – August 2026) and the Powers of Pain 2026 draft grades. Player movement cross-checked against the SCFL trade ledger and POP's contemporaneous trade posts. Tyson injury reporting per national NFL coverage, August 17, 2026. Two obscenities softened for the magazine; the sentiment is unaltered.

investigations.headline: Some Records Are Made Up
investigations.subhead: The 1,600-yard lie, the mask, the microfilm, and the apology that never came.
paragraphs: It began the way most SCFL disasters begin: with a man reminiscing about a football team that was not very good. The subject was Lakeland High, class of 1997. The man was Creams — known in these chats, for reasons lost to time and better left there, as Dwayne. And Dwayne had a number.
Sixteen hundred yards. Receiving. Six games. Senior year.

There are lies, and there are lies with a paper trail, and Dwayne — God bless him — volunteered the paper trail. “The stats are in the newspaper at the library,” he said. “North County News, 1997. You don’t live far from the library. Go look it up.”
He was talking to the wrong man. He was talking to Keith.

Keith runs The Machines. He runs the power rankings. He is a four-time champion and the single most relentless voice in a chat that has never once lacked for volume. When Keith is told that the truth is sitting on a roll of microfilm eleven minutes from his house, Keith does not text back. Keith gets his keys.

There was, to be fair, a math problem. Sixteen hundred receiving yards in a season is not a “good year.” It is a New York State record. It is the kind of number that makes a seventeen-year-old the most recruited receiver in the country. It had never, the chat quickly established, been sniffed by anyone out of Lakeland — a program that spent that fall getting run off the field.

It was August 2021. There was a pandemic on. The library turned Keith away at the door for not wearing a mask. Keith found a mask. Keith went back. Keith explained to the woman at the desk exactly why a grown man needed the 1997 North County News on microfilm — and, in his words, “she even had some words for Dwayne herself.”
Then he started to spin. Reel by reel. Game by game. Photographing every Lakeland football item the paper printed that fall and posting them to the chat in real time, like a hostage video.

The findings were not kind. Lakeland went 1–7. In one game the entire team gained roughly 260 yards — total, all eleven of them. The other schools got write-ups; Lakeland got a blurb, and one week the blurb was faded enough that Dwayne would later claim his real numbers had been, conveniently, blacked out. Dwayne’s actual senior receiving total, per the North County News: 593 yards. The individual lines surfaced too. “Dwayne — 62 yards.” “I’ll give Dwayne all 29 of them.”
Five hundred and ninety-three. He had said sixteen hundred.

The chat, sensing blood and microfilm, ascended. “He could have dialed www dot Google dot com,” Sheq marveled, “but the man got a mask, went around roadblocks, just to prove Dwayne wrong — and Dwayne STILL won’t admit it.” PCE was more clinical: “Keith went to the library and your butthole got super tight.” Keith, doing the math on his own crime scene, offered a theory of the case: “593 actually equals 1600 if you factor in interest since 1997.” Collars co-signed the accounting: “that’s a pro-rated 1600.”

Dwayne’s rebuttal was a masterclass in every direction but backward. He wondered aloud whether Keith had doctored 1997 microfilm. He pivoted to vaccines. He explained that Lakeland was “a bullshit program” next to the real powers — throwing his own school under the bus to account for why a record-setting year went unnoticed. He pointed out — correctly, irrelevantly — that PCE also claims a fictional stolen-base record and Jay a phantom Lakeland home-run record, as if a chat full of liars somehow exonerates the biggest one. Then he went dark for days.

Keith would not allow it. “Day 1,” he posted. “Waiting for the 1600-yard lie to be addressed, or an apology.” Then Day 2. Then Day 3. It got a name — 1600 Gate — and a proposed sentence: a formal vote to rename Dwayne’s franchise “The 1600s,” in perpetuity, until he confessed.

He never quite did. Five days in, cornered, Dwayne produced the closest thing to a white flag the SCFL has ever recorded: “I was wrong about 1600 being my senior season total. If that’s what I said. I remember seeing an article with my yards amount, and it said 1600.” Beavers offered the kindest available theory: “Maybe it was 1600 points. Your senior season. Of basketball.”

Keith called off the dogs. He did not, and this is the entire point, forget. Four years later “microfiche” remains the most feared word in the chat — the thing you reach for when you want to call a man’s bluff and mean it. There have been sequels. There have been threats to rename the last-place team “Microfiche” for a season. There has been, from Dwayne, no correction.

Because that is the thing about a league that keeps its own history — that will take an hour out of a workday to go check the record. Some records are made to be broken. This one was made up. And the North County News, 1997, is still on file.

investigations.headline: Not Guilty of Cheating. Guilty of Being Good.
investigations.subhead: For twenty-one years the league has whispered that The Machines rig it. We pulled every trade. Here is what the ledger actually says.
paragraphs: There is a theory of the Skirt Chasers Fantasy League that has survived longer than most of the franchises in it. The theory is simple and it is repeated, in some form, every single autumn: Keith cheats. The Machines are the Evil Empire. He preys on the weak owners, he collects the rebuilders like toll booths, and the rest of the league is left to split the scraps he does not want. It is a good story. It has a villain, it has victims, and it explains — cleanly, comfortably — why the same team keeps ending up on top. This newsroom decided to do the one thing nobody in twenty-one years of group chat had bothered to do. We pulled the receipts.

The record itself is not in dispute, and it is the reason the theory exists at all. The Machines are 215-63 across the tracked era — a .773 winning percentage in a league where nobody else is above .600. Twenty playoff appearances in twenty-one seasons. Four championships, nine runner-up finishes, an all-play record (3,198-944) that reads like a typo. You do not have to like it to respect it, and most of the league has chosen the first option. When a team is that good for that long, the human brain does not reach for "well-run." It reaches for "rigged." That instinct is the entire case for the prosecution, and it is worth taking seriously — so we did.

The charge, stated plainly, is collusion: that Keith wins because a handful of soft, compliant owners feed him their best players for pennies. If that were true, it would leave a fingerprint. Collusion is narrow by nature — you cannot conspire with the whole room. So we mapped every trade The Machines have made in the available ledger: forty-five deals, laid end to end, sorted by who was standing on the other side of the table.

The fingerprint is not there. Across those forty-five trades, The Machines dealt with fifteen different franchises — which is to say, effectively everyone who has held a roster in the modern league. The most frequent partner was Wookie Leaks, with sixteen deals. Second was Lil’ Chops at thirteen. But right behind them sit New World Order (nine) — a seventeen-time playoff team — the Smoke Dragons (eight), Pork Chop Express (eight), the Heavy Hitters (seven), Powers of Pain (seven), and the Killer Klowns (seven). Powers of Pain owns more championships than Keith does. New World Order has made the playoffs more often than all but one team in the league. These are not patsies. This is not a cabal of three. This is a man doing business with the entire building.

This is where the prosecution’s case quietly changes shape. Confronted with the spread, the charge stops being "he only trades with weaklings" and becomes "he beats everyone he trades with" — which is not a crime. That is just trading well. And trading well, it turns out, is the thing Keith actually does. He is not stealing players in the dark. He is standing in the open market every summer, making more offers than anyone else, and being right slightly more often than he is wrong. Over forty-five deals the pattern is not a series of heists; it is a decent batting average compounded over two decades.

Consider the mechanics the theory leaves out. In a dynasty league, the rebuilders are not victims of the contender — they are the contender’s trading partners by design. A team going nowhere in November has one asset that a title team wants (a productive veteran) and one thing it needs (young picks). Keith buys the veteran; the rebuilder banks the pick and the promise of next year. Both sides walk away having gotten the thing they came for. When Wookie Leaks — a franchise still hunting its first playoff berth — moves a win-now piece to The Machines for draft capital, that is not Keith fleecing Wookie. That is Wookie doing precisely what a rebuilding team is supposed to do, with the one buyer reliably willing to pay.

Does he win the deals? Often, yes. Our read of the ledger is that The Machines come out ahead on the clear majority of their trades, roughly even on a handful, and genuinely behind on only one or two. That is an elite hit rate, and it is exactly what you would expect from the best evaluator in a league of friends who mostly trade on vibes and grudges. But "wins most of his trades" and "cheats" are not the same sentence, no matter how many times they get said in the same breath.

And the losses matter, because they are the part the theory cannot survive. If Keith were rigging outcomes, he would not have a loss column. He does. The cleanest one is almost funny: he traded a young tight end away, watched the kid turn into exactly what everyone feared, and had to circle back two years later and buy the same player back at full price. That is not the ledger of a man with the game in a fix. That is the ledger of a very good manager who is still, occasionally, human — which is the most exculpatory evidence we found.

So why does the accusation never die? Because it does useful work for the fourteen other guys. "Keith cheats" is a more bearable explanation than "Keith is better than me at the one thing we all show up to do." The persecution complex Keith wears — everyone’s teaming up on me, they gang up because I’m the best — is not entirely paranoia; the chat does organize against him, does root against him, does treat a deal that helps The Machines as a threat to the republic. But that is a tax the league levies on excellence, not evidence of a crime. They gang up on him because he keeps winning. He keeps winning because he is good.

This newsroom has now read every deal, counted every partner, and weighed the one asset the prosecution never brings to the table: a motive that holds up. There is no cabal. There is no soft underbelly he feeds on to the exclusion of everyone else. There is a market, open every summer, and one man who works it harder and reads it better than the rest of the room — and a room that has decided, for twenty-one years, that this must be against the rules.

The verdict of the ledger is not close. On the charge of cheating: not guilty. On the charge of collusion: not guilty. On the charge of being, by a wide and infuriating margin, the best trader and the best manager this league has produced — guilty, and it is not up for appeal. File it under the only heading that fits. Some empires are built in the dark. This one was built in the group chat, in broad daylight, one fair deal at a time, while everybody watched and nobody could stop it.

investigations.headline: The Players Who Died Waiting
investigations.subhead: The Gumbas doesn't lose trades. He never makes them — the offers land on read, the deals die at the altar, and the stars rot on his roster.
paragraphs: There are a hundred ways to torch a dynasty in this league, and most of them are loud — a butchered draft, a waiver-wire panic, the occasional trade so lopsided it earns its own investigation. The Gumbas has spent years perfecting the hundred-and-first, and it is completely silent: do nothing, and let it kill you by inches.

Start with the phone. For years the offers came in — real ones, generous ones, for the best names on his roster — and for years they got the same answer: none. Messages sat read and unreturned. A video call once rang out into the void. When he did bother to reply, it was to explain he “hadn't even thought about football.” In a league that lives and dies in the group chat, one manager treats every incoming deal like a number he doesn't recognize.

And understand — this was never lowball junk he was right to ignore. On one November night the table in front of him held four draft picks and two starters for a single receiver, a haul so heavy the man across from him started chasing down a second first-round pick just to sweeten it further. Blockbuster money. Franchise-altering. He looked at all of it, and he blinked.

His own words, typed at one in the morning after that night, are the thesis of the entire case: “all good offers — I might kick myself tomorrow — but think it's smart for me to wait.” He did not, for the record, wait for a better offer. He waited for no offer. He waited until the asset wasn't worth trading at all.

Once he even said yes. “Take out the second-round pick,” he wrote, “and let's do it” — handshake emoji and all. The deal still didn't close. When a man can't finish a trade he has already agreed to in writing, the terms were never the problem. It's the trigger, and the pulling of it.

And when he does negotiate, he knows exactly one direction: toward himself. Handed a fair slate of picks for his quarterback, his instinct wasn't to accept or counter — it was to try to slip an extra player onto his own side of the ledger, and then to admit, when it collapsed, that “if you said no I would have just taken the three picks.” A man who'll accept a deal only if you stop improving it isn't a shark circling the table. He's driftwood with a roster.
But the cold feet are only the symptom. Here is the disease, the one that shows up in the standings every single year: he will not sell a star while the star is still worth a damn.

Every asset in dynasty has a window. You move the aging back, the receiver on the wrong side of the hill, the quarterback with one good season left — you move him while somebody out there still believes in the name. The Gumbas can't do it. He'd rather admire the nameplate than cash the value it's bleeding by the week.

You don't have to theorize about where that leads, because there's a body. Nick Chubb sat on his roster straight through the window a smart manager sells in. He was told, plainly and in real time, that the price was peaking and about to slide. He held. By the time it came up again the verdict was in — a back with a wrecked knee and a career all but over, worth, in the honest read of the room, nothing. He didn't sell Chubb high. He didn't sell Chubb low. He held Chubb all the way to zero.

And he knew, somewhere. Warned to move his prize receiver before the man went the way of Chubb, he waved it off: “gonna sell him when the price is really high — lol, jk.” The “jk” was the whole tragedy. He never sold high. He never sold at all.

Hill, Kittle, Stafford — the same marquee names, dangled and chased across three separate seasons, the same November dance, the same non-answer every time. Each one a player he could have cashed at the top of the market. Each one held a beat too long, then a season too long, then for good. The receiver aged out of his prime. The tight end crept past the wrong side of thirty. The quarterback turned thirty-six with his best years plainly behind him. He watched all of it happen in real time and did nothing but hit “seen.”

THE LEDGER — and here the market speaks for itself, because these aren't spreadsheet estimates. They're the offers he was actually quoted, and turned down. For Tyreek Hill alone the table once held a top-three first-round pick, three second-rounders, and two starting receivers — with a second first-rounder being lined up to close it. That is better than two first-round picks for one man, and he let it walk out the door. Matthew Stafford was quoted a first and a second. George Kittle carried a first in his own right. And Nick Chubb, at his peak, was a first-round back before the knee turned him to dust. Add up the real market he was shown — not a model, the actual packages on his phone — and the stars he sat on were worth the better part of seven first-round picks: a genuine franchise's worth of ammunition. Today those same four names are worth, combined, about a single second-round pick. He didn't lose a trade war. He refused to show up to it — and the bill came due anyway.

He'll tell you he's rebuilding. He has been “rebuilding” for years — a permanent, load-bearing excuse that has never once required him to actually make the trade a rebuild is built on. You cannot rebuild by hoarding aging veterans and leaving the picks people hand you unopened in your inbox. That isn't a rebuild. It's a hostage situation, and he's the one who won't negotiate.

So the window closes, the way windows do, and the end state is a roster that reads like a hospice ward: a row of names that used to mean something, kept comfortable, dealt to no one, quietly expiring in the starting lineup. They weren't traded. They weren't cut. They died of natural causes, on his watch, waiting on a call he was too scared to make.

He'll call it patience. The tape calls it something else. Patience is holding out for the right price; this is a man so terrified of the wrong move that he has mastered the art of no move at all — and then points at the corpses and calls it depth. Somewhere on that roster tonight is a player worth more today than he will ever be worth again. The Gumbas knows it. He'll hold him anyway. And come winter, the NewsRoom will be back to identify the body.

investigations.headline: The Template Case: How an SCFL Investigation Gets Built
investigations.subhead: Steal this structure. Change the facts. Bring receipts.
paragraphs: THE COLD OPEN. Start with the single most damning fact you have, stated plainly, with no windup. One sentence that makes a manager put his phone down. Example: 'For three straight seasons, one franchise has left more points on its bench than half the league scored.'
THE STAKES. One short paragraph on why anyone should care: what it cost, who it hurt, what it says about the league. This is where you name the teams involved — always teams, never real names.

THE RECEIPTS. The middle of an investigation is evidence, not opinion. Pull from the record book, the box scores, the chat archive. Two or three paragraphs, each built around one verifiable fact. If you can't verify it, it doesn't go in — say 'the record shows' only when the record actually shows it.

THE OTHER SIDE. Give the accused franchise its say, even if its say is ridiculous. Quote the chat if they've commented. If they haven't: 'The franchise did not respond to repeated requests for comment' is a beautiful sentence and always true.
THE TURN. The best SCFL investigations end by zooming out: what this means for the standings, the record book, or the August vote. Leave one question deliberately unanswered — that's your sequel.

HOW TO FILE IT. Write yours at the Water Cooler desk (feed it a chat export or write it straight), then Office → Send to HQ. The Commissioner runs it through the Newsroom and it publishes with your byline.
